analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on very large estates and gifts from 40% to 20%.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the top tax rate on estates, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers from 40% to 20%, retroactive to the start of 2021. The estate tax only applies to very large inheritances, so the main beneficiaries would be heirs to the wealthiest families. The bill also exempted its own revenue loss from budget pay-as-you-go rules. It was referred to two House committees but was never taken up, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates and wealthy families making large taxable gifts. The estate tax under current law applies only to estates above a large exemption (roughly $11.7 million per person in 2021), so a cut from 40% to 20% would go overwhelmingly to the top fraction of one percent of inheritances.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets the rate of tax on estates, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers at 20%, down from the current top rate of 40%.
The cut would be retroactive, applying to estates of people dying and gifts made after December 31, 2020.
The bill exempts its budgetary effects from the statutory PAYGO scorecards, so the lost revenue would not trigger automatic spending offsets under those rules.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers broadly, who would have to make up billions in lost estate and gift tax revenue or see deficits rise. Because the bill exempted itself from PAYGO, the cost would not be offset.

drawbacks.text: The federal estate tax touches only the largest estates — in 2021, the first $11.7 million per person was already exempt — so a rate cut from 40% to 20% would deliver nearly all of its benefit to very large inheritances while reducing revenue that funds the government for everyone else.
The bill exempts its own budgetary effects from the pay-as-you-go scorecards, meaning the lost revenue would not be offset by spending cuts or other taxes under those rules.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the estate tax is one of the most progressive taxes in the code, paid by a very small share of decedents' estates, so reducing its rate is a targeted tax cut rather than broad tax relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated and large: wealthy families with taxable estates could pass on substantially more. The cost is diffuse — lost federal revenue, unoffset under PAYGO by the bill's own terms. Since only the largest estates pay the tax, the gains and losses fall on opposite ends of the wealth scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Budget committees in May 2021, the committees never took it up, and it expired at the end of the 117th Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 13, 2021 by Rep. Jodey Arrington with two cosponsors, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D) and Rep. Charles Fleischmann (R).
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Budget Committee.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Only two members cosponsored the bill across the entire two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No concentrated interest gained, because the rate cut never happened; the biggest beneficiary of the bill's failure is the federal Treasury, which kept the 40% estate tax rate and the revenue it raises from the largest estates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; the tax cut never happened

for.name: Rep. Jodey Arrington
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the estate and gift tax rate to 20% and referred it to Ways and Means and Budget.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and one cosponsor were Republicans and one cosponsor was a Democrat, but the bill drew only three total supporters and no party pushed for a vote.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates and ultrawealthy families
industries.note: A 40%-to-20% cut on estates above roughly $11.7 million per person (2021 exemption) would let the wealthiest families keep far more of their inheritances, while the lost revenue would otherwise be paid by taxpayers broadly. The bill died, so no gain occurred.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory industry
industries.note: A lower transfer-tax rate changes estate planning strategies and could reduce demand for tax-driven planning while giving planners a new rule change to market around. This is a minor, indirect effect.
